questions.stem: What does a bubble potometer measure directly?

options.text: The uptake of water by the shoot
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The mass lost by the plant
options.explanation: That is the mass potometer's reading.
Humidity is a factor tested, not the measurement.
Stomatal aperture is not recorded by any potometer.

questions.stem: What does a mass potometer measure directly?

options.explanation: Temperature is a tested factor, not the reading.

options.text: The change in mass of the plant as water evaporates
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
That belongs to the bubble potometer.
The shoot sits in the potometer, out of soil.

questions.stem: Why can water uptake stand in for water loss?

options.text: Because the potometer adds water chemically
options.explanation: Nothing chemical replaces the loss.

options.text: Because uptake and loss are unrelated
options.explanation: They track each other through the water column.

options.text: The continuous water column means each evaporated molecule pulls a replacement up the stem
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Leaves do not hoard the incoming water.

questions.stem: Which environmental factors can this practical test?

options.explanation: Those affect growth, not this evaporation measurement.
Neither is an environmental factor in the set.
Wind is one of four factors, not the only one.

options.text: Light intensity, air movement, humidity and temperature
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

questions.stem: Which piece of kit sets the light intensity in this investigation?

options.text: A lamp placed at measured distances from the shoot
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
A fan varies air movement, not light.
The bag raises humidity.
It reads temperature; it does not set it.

questions.stem: Name the two potometer types and what each records.
questions.modelAnswer: A mass potometer records mass change; a bubble potometer records water uptake.

questions.stem: List the apparatus for the light-intensity version of the practical.
questions.modelAnswer: Potometer, timer, lamp, ruler and plant.

questions.stem: Explain why the shoot is cut underwater before assembly.
questions.modelAnswer: Cutting underwater stops air entering the xylem, since an air lock would break the continuous water column and stall the flow.

questions.stem: A student wants to test wind speed instead of light. Name the factor they change and one control they must keep.
questions.modelAnswer: They change the air movement, for example with a fan, while keeping temperature or humidity controlled.

questions.stem: Why are the leaves dried before readings begin?

options.explanation: Cleanliness is not the reason cited.

options.text: Surface water would evaporate too and inflate the apparent transpiration
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Drying reduces mass; the point is fairness.
Drying does not close stomata.

questions.stem: How long does the plant adapt at each lamp distance?

options.explanation: Days belong to the respiration flask run.
Skipping adaptation leaves stomata unadjusted.
Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Thirty minutes is the timing window for the bubble, not adaptation.

questions.stem: How is the bubble's distance converted into a rate?

options.explanation: Multiplication inverts the rate logic.
Unrelated quantities cannot subtract.
That is the inverse of the rate.

options.text: Distance moved by the bubble divided by the 30-minute period
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: How is the air bubble reset between runs?

options.text: By opening the reservoir tap to move the bubble back
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: By cutting a new shoot each time
options.explanation: The same shoot is reused across distances.

options.text: By refilling the capillary with ink
options.explanation: No ink is involved.

options.text: By waiting for it to drift back
options.explanation: The tap, not patience, resets it.

questions.stem: What seals the gaps in the assembled potometer?

options.explanation: Cotton wool insulates flasks; it does not seal potometers.
Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Tape is not the named sealant.
Rubber bungs alone leak; jelly completes the seal.

questions.stem: State the three lamp distances used in the method.
questions.modelAnswer: The lamp sits at 10 cm, then 20 cm, then 40 cm from the leaf.

questions.stem: State the formula used to obtain the transpiration rate.
questions.modelAnswer: Rate of transpiration equals the distance moved by the bubble divided by the time period of 30 minutes.

questions.stem: Explain why repeats at each distance are taken before moving the lamp.
questions.modelAnswer: Repeats reveal anomalies and let a mean be taken, so one odd run cannot masquerade as the effect of the new distance.

questions.stem: A bubble travels 32 mm in 30 minutes. Compute the rate and give its units.
questions.modelAnswer: 32 divided by 30 gives about 1.07 mm per minute.

questions.stem: What pattern did the results table show between lamp distance and bubble travel?

options.explanation: The three rows show a clear descending pattern.
The 40 cm row moved only 12 mm.

options.text: Closer lamp, greater bubble movement, higher rate
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The 10 cm run moved 32 mm, the largest travel.

questions.stem: Why does bright light raise the transpiration rate?

options.explanation: Light acts through the stomata, not by radiating the water away.
No thickening occurs during the run.
The bubble tracks uptake, not light pressure.

options.text: More stomata open, so more water vapour escapes
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: Which flaw mixes two variables in this design?

options.text: The lamp warms the shoot, so temperature varies alongside light intensity
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: The bubble is too small to see
options.explanation: The bubble is visible; that is not the cited flaw.
Measurement is fine; the confounding is the issue.
Shoots survive well enough for the 30-minute runs.

questions.stem: How can an air-blocked xylem be avoided?

options.explanation: Light is irrelevant to the blockage.

options.text: Cut the stem underwater and assemble the equipment underwater too
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Blow through the stem to clear it
options.explanation: Blowing adds what it claims to remove.
Thickness does not prevent air entry.

questions.stem: Which room factors drift during the experiment and threaten validity?

options.explanation: Equipment economics is not an experimental factor.
Those are held constant by the CORMS design.
Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Neither varies meaningfully indoors.

questions.stem: State the three rates recorded in the results table.
questions.modelAnswer: 1.07, 0.80 and 0.40 mm per minute at 10, 20 and 40 cm.

questions.stem: Name two fixable faults listed in the limitations.
questions.modelAnswer: Imperfect seals that leak, and blockages in the plant cutting.

questions.stem: Explain why the result at 10 cm may overstate the pure light effect.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the closest lamp also heats the shoot most, so part of the measured rise comes from temperature rather than from light intensity alone.

questions.stem: Propose one improvement to isolate light from temperature in this practical.
questions.modelAnswer: Place a heat filter or a water screen between lamp and shoot, or use a cool LED source, so light intensity changes while temperature stays level.

questions.stem: How is humidity increased in the further experiments?

options.text: By pointing a fan at the shoot
options.explanation: A fan changes air movement, not humidity.

options.text: By moving the plant to a cold room
options.explanation: Rooms change temperature.
Drying lowers local humidity, if anything.

options.text: Spray water into a plastic bag and wrap it around the plant
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: In the CORMS frame for the light trial, what is the Organisms requirement?

options.text: The same species, size, age and number of leaves in every repeat
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Any plant available at the time
options.explanation: Unmatched shoots break the fair test.
The same shoot is reused.
Removing leaves changes the organism itself.

questions.stem: What is measured in the CORMS Measurement slot for the light trial?

options.explanation: Height is irrelevant to this measurement.

options.text: The distance the bubble travels, in 30 minutes
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The lamp supplies the change, not the reading.
Temperature belongs to the Same list.

questions.stem: Which factor is investigated with a hairdryer?

options.explanation: The lamp investigates light.
Soil temperature is not this shoot's tested factor.
Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
A hairdryer moves air; misted bags raise humidity.

questions.stem: Why must temperature, wind and humidity sit in the Same list for the light trial?

options.text: Because they are impossible to measure
options.explanation: They are measurable; they must merely stay fixed.

options.text: Because they have no effect on transpiration
options.explanation: They affect it strongly, which is exactly why they must be held.

options.text: Because the CORMS letters must all be used
options.explanation: Letters earn their place by role, not by quota.

options.text: So the changed factor is the only systematic difference between runs
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: State how temperature is varied in the further experiments.
questions.modelAnswer: By running the practical in a cold room or a warm room.

questions.stem: Expand the CORMS acronym.
Explain why the plastic-bag method tests humidity without starving the shoot.
questions.modelAnswer: The bag encloses the air around the leaves, raising its humidity, while the stem still draws water from the potometer reservoir, so the shoot stays supplied.

questions.stem: Draft a CORMS plan for the humidity variant.
questions.modelAnswer: Change the bag's internal humidity; keep the same shoot species, size and leaves; repeat each condition; measure bubble distance in 30 minutes; hold temperature, light and airflow the same.
